title: Levitating magnet at 138 million rpm opens the door to dark matter
excerpt: Scientists in Singapore manage to levitate a 30-micron magnet over superconducting lead and spin it at 138 million rpm, a record for these systems, opening the way to studying dark matter.
content:
A team from the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore, led by Tao Wang, has levitated a spherical neodymium iron boron magnet about 30 microns in size over superconducting lead at about -269 degrees. The magnetically levitated rotor spins at 138 million revolutions per minute, the highest figure recorded to date in this type of system.

Low friction and stability for vacuum and magnetic field sensors 🔬

The key to the system lies in its low friction and stability: the speed drops by 50 percent in 17 days, which makes it possible to maintain the rotation for long periods without intervention. That combination turns the rotor into a highly sensitive sensor of vacuum and magnetic fields. The finding opens avenues for searching for dark matter, detecting gravitational waves and exploring quantum effects under laboratory conditions.

A magnet that spins faster than your kitchen blender 🌀

One hundred thirty-eight million revolutions per minute sounds like a mark worthy of a competition, but no one here is going to break speed records for fun. The magnet spins so fast and so stably that it serves to hunt for dark matter, even though the TV remote still fails to turn up at home. At least this rotor does not complain about the cold at -269 degrees.
